l: Retrieving, Rethinking and Revising: The Chain-of-Verification Can Improve Retrieval Augmented Generation, Retrieving, Rethinking and Revising: The Chain-of-Verification Can Improve Retrieval Augmented Generation, 4 / Results and Analysis / 4.1 / Main Results .. 4.4 / Further Analysis on Retriever
s: This unit evaluates CoV-RAG, a retrieval-augmented generation method, on open-domain question answering across Natural Questions, WebQuestions, Mintaka, and TriviaQA. CoV-RAG outperforms WebGLM and other comparison methods, with multi-iteration CoV-RAG achieving the strongest results across the tested models and datasets. Ablation studies find that revising after retrieval and using a score-to-judge-to-revise Chain of Verification structure improve performance. GPT-4-based evaluation further reports that CoV-RAG achieves better citation, correctness, truthfulness, bias, and conciseness results, while multi-iteration retrieval improves retrieval accuracy with Bing and Chrome.

s: CoV-RAG outperforms GPT-3, RRR, ChatGPT, Self-RAG, Perplexity.ai, and WebGLM across the reported open-domain question-answering results. Its multi-iteration version generally outperforms CoV-RAG-S, and its performance improves through end-stage revision, a score-to-judge-to-revise chain, and re-retrieval.

s: The unit discusses hallucinations in large language models and methods for addressing them, including detection, data augmentation, and retrieval-augmented generation. l: TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: “TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation,” by Jinyuan Fang, Zaiqiao Meng, and Craig Macdonald of the University of Glasgow, is an EMNLP 2024 Findings paper on improving retrieval-augmented generation for multi-hop question answering. It addresses the problem that retrieved Wikipedia document sets contain substantial irrelevant or noisy material. Given a question and retrieved documents, TRACE first uses a Knowledge Graph Generator to turn documents into knowledge triples, then uses a triple ranker and LLM-based autoregressive selector to construct logically connected reasoning chains. These chains either become the answer generator’s context (TRACE-Triple) or identify and order a smaller set of useful original documents (TRACE-Doc). Beam search, multiple candidate chains, and adaptive chain termination support the process. The paper evaluates TRACE on HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, whose questions require two to four reasoning hops. TRACE-Triple and TRACE-Doc outperform naive RAG, document-ranking methods, and IRCoT; compared with using all retrieved documents, they improve Exact Match by average margins of 14.03% and 13.46%, respectively. TRACE-Triple often attains strong results with substantially fewer context tokens, while TRACE-Doc achieves the best reported performance among listed systems with Mistral-7B-v0.1. Ablations find that the KG generator, chain constructor, triple ranker, triple selector, demonstrations, suitable chain counts, and adaptive termination all matter. Adaptive chain lengths outperform fixed four-step chains by avoiding redundant triples. Further analyses report that HotPotQA graphs average 83.21 entities and 79.06 triples, while chains average about three steps and identify about 2.6 documents; these selected documents have much lower error rates than the original retrieved sets. Case studies show that multiple chains can provide complementary evidence and avoid noisy documents. TRACE has higher indexing latency than IRCoT because it generates triples, but comparable or lower inference runtime because its selector uses a single token rather than generating multi-token thoughts. The paper concludes that grounded reasoning chains generalize across reader models, while noting limits: Wikipedia-focused retrieval, unavailable annotations for directly evaluating triples and chains, title-to-text-entity-focused triples, and a black-box LLM setting that may yield only one chain without selector logits.

l: reasoning chains, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Reasoning chains are series of logically connected knowledge-graph triples constructed from documents Dq to answer a question q. Their central role is to identify and integrate supporting evidence: they can serve directly as context for generating an answer or identify relevant supporting documents while avoiding irrelevant or noisy ones. In TRACE, a constructor selects triples autoregressively according to the question and previously selected triples, preserving coherence and grounding the chains in retrieved documents. Construction proceeds iteratively, maintaining multiple candidate chains and retaining those with the highest cumulative scores. A chain can terminate once its selected triples are sufficient to answer the question; its required length may be determined adaptively. Multiple chains may contribute complementary information absent from an initial chain, creating enriched context and initially improving performance, although excessive length can introduce redundant or irrelevant information and degrade performance. Across datasets, chains average approximately three steps and identify about 2.6 relevant documents from Dq. Adaptive-length chains outperform chains fixed at length 4. Their grounding is intended to make reasoning more reliable and accurate than potentially inaccurate generated CoT sentences, and they generalise across reader models. Because annotated data is unavailable, the chains themselves are not directly and quantitatively evaluated; instead, their effectiveness is assessed through final QA performance, statistics, and qualitative results.

l: retrieval-augmented generation, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-augmented generation is a generation method and an effective approach for question answering and knowledge-intensive NLP tasks. It typically unfolds as a retriever-reader pipeline: a retriever obtains relevant information, then a reader generates answers from retrieved documents. It has shown strong QA performance and has been used for multi-hop questions and, in some applications, knowledge graph question answering. Its central limitation is retriever imperfection: irrelevant documents may be included and hinder answers. In the vanilla RAG baseline, all retrieved documents are given to the reader; TRACE-Triple and TRACE-Doc substantially improve on this baseline while often using less context.

l: question answering, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Question answering (QA) is the task on which retrieval-augmented generation models have achieved strong performance. The unit focuses on improving QA for multi-hop questions by identifying and integrating supporting evidence. Question answering research in the unit includes open-domain, multi-hop, knowledge-base, and knowledge-intensive settings. The cited methods use passage retrieval, generative models, knowledge graphs, graph reasoning, and unified structured and unstructured representations.

l: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RAG models use a retriever-reader architecture, with retrieved documents supporting answer generation and large language models reading documents prepended to questions. They achieve remarkable QA performance but can degrade when irrelevant retrieval adds noise, especially in multi-hop reasoning. TRACE addresses this by constructing knowledge-grounded reasoning chains from retrieved documents.

s: Multi-hop questions are questions requiring multiple reasoning steps to obtain correct answers. They are central to this work and are represented by a question, answer, and retrieved documents. Because irrelevant retrieved information can degrade retrieval-augmented generation performance, TRACE constructs evidence chains across documents.

l: TRACE, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: TRACE is a framework and method for improving the multi-hop reasoning ability of retrieval-augmented generation models and for identifying supporting evidence in retrieved documents. It processes a multi-hop question without requiring training, using in-context learning to mitigate effects of irrelevant documents. First, its Knowledge Graph Generator independently transforms retrieved documents into a knowledge graph, reducing the lost-in-the-middle issue. Second, its novel Autoregressive Reasoning Chain Constructor iteratively selects connected knowledge-graph triples to build knowledge-grounded reasoning chains. It uses an adaptive chain-termination strategy to determine chain lengths; adaptive-length chains significantly outperform fixed-length chains. Finally, a reader uses the chains directly for answer generation or uses them to select useful documents, supporting triple-based and document-based answer generation. TRACE uses prompts to generate triples, select triples, and generate answers; LLaMA3-7B can generate thoughts or select triples, while LLaMA3, Mistral-7B-v0.1, and Gemma-7B are used as readers. It requires triple-selector logits to define a triple distribution. If logits are unavailable, it can select one triple per step with an option token, producing a single reasoning chain. Across HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue in a zero-shot setting, TRACE-Triple improved average Exact Match by 14.03% over using all retrieved documents, while TRACE-Doc improved it by 13.46%; Exact Match and F1 score are metrics. Its chains generalize across readers. Generating knowledge-graph triples adds indexing cost, measured as 12.34 seconds on HotPotQA development sets, but triple selection with one token helps inference; its HotPotQA inference runtime is 4.13 seconds and is similar to IRCoT there and lower on 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue.

l: supporting evidence, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Supporting evidence is information in documents that directly helps answer questions. TRACE identifies it in retrieved documents by converting text into fine-grained knowledge triples and autoregressively selecting connected, grounded triples, reducing irrelevant context and improving answer accuracy.

l: documents, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The entity is retrieved documents supplied as potential evidence for answering questions. They are obtained with a retriever model, often from Wikipedia, and each has a title and text. Datasets provide relevant and irrelevant documents, randomly shuffled in their original order, with annotations of relevance; using all of them as context can therefore introduce noise. TRACE converts the documents into knowledge triples, extracts reasoning chains, and uses those chains to identify a useful subset. The selected documents contain much less noise than the originals: in the HotPotQA test set, their error rate is 21.06%, versus 79.66% for the original documents.

l: KG Generator, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: KG Generator is a TRACE component that creates a knowledge graph from retrieved documents. It uses an LLM with in-context learning to generate knowledge triples independently for each document, receiving a document and outputting identified triples. For Wikipedia documents, it treats the title as an entity and extracts entities in the text and their relationships with that title. It primarily generates triples between titles and text entities rather than between all entities, simplifying the task and mitigating the lost-in-the-middle issue. Its prompts use demonstrations from 50 manually labelled training documents per dataset, with E5-Mistral retrieving three similar examples. It is evaluated through sentence- and document-based variants; sentences perform better on all three reported datasets.

l: knowledge graph, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The knowledge graph is a structured knowledge representation: a set of concise, fine-grained triples, each consisting of a head entity, relation, and tail entity. In TRACE, it is generated by the Knowledge Graph Generator from question-associated retrieved documents, rather than from an existing knowledge graph. Algorithm 1 initializes the graph and adds triples generated independently from each retrieved document; relationships across documents are formed through entities shared among them. The graph is the basis for constructing reasoning chains and for identifying relevant evidence, providing a solid foundation for subsequent reasoning through reliable document grounding. Its main value is that triples give a more concise and fine-grained representation than sentences or whole documents: replacing the graph with either significantly reduces performance. Qualitative results on HotPotQA indicate generally high-quality, document-grounded triples with minimal hallucination. The graphs are nevertheless highly sparse because cross-document relationships can be difficult or meaningless to infer, leaving entities with fewer connections. Their size and density vary across HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue; on the HotPotQA test set, they average 83.21 entities, 79.06 triples, and 1.20% density. They are also reported in Table 5 for the experimental datasets.

l: Autoregressive Reasoning Chain Constructor, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Autoregressive Reasoning Chain Constructor is a component of TRACE that builds novel, knowledge-grounded reasoning chains from a knowledge graph to support question answering. It unfolds autoregressively: at each step, it selects a logically connected knowledge triple based on the question and earlier triples, retrieves candidates with a bi-encoder triple ranker, and chooses a triple with an LLM-based selector. Beam search produces multiple chains, including top-5 chains, and chains may terminate when no further triples are needed. Demonstrations in the prompt guide construction; they are retrieved as the three most similar questions from manually labelled training questions. Its effectiveness is evaluated through TRACE-Doc and variants involving triple counts and demonstrations. A limitation is that the triple selector may be a black-box LLM.

l: reader, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The reader is a component that generates answers from questions and prepended context, including selected documents or reasoning chains. Prompted for zero-shot in-context learning, it is instructed to output only an answer grounded in that context and uses greedy decoding. It is used with baseline-selected documents, then varied with Mistral-7B-v0.1 and Gemma-7B to test whether TRACE reasoning chains generalize across models, with similar results to LLaMA3.

l: large language models (LLMs), TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large language models (LLMs) have powerful in-context learning capabilities but are prone to hallucinate. Used as readers in retrieval-augmented generation, TRACE prompts them to generate knowledge graphs and construct autoregressive reasoning chains; research also examines retrieval, reasoning, extraction, graphs, distraction, and temporal reasoning.

l: triples, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Knowledge triples express single factual units as a head entity, relation, and tail entity. TRACE extracts or generates them from input and retrieved documents as concise candidate knowledge, reducing irrelevant information when finding supporting evidence. TRACE-Triple uses them to build reasoning chains: a triple ranker assesses relevance and a triple selector guides use and extends paths toward answers. Removing or replacing these components significantly harms performance. The triples are primarily formed between titles and entities in Wikipedia texts, and their quality is not directly or quantitatively evaluated because annotated data is unavailable. Adaptive chain termination determines how many triples a chain needs, avoiding unnecessary, redundant triples and improving performance.

l: TRACE-Triple, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: TRACE-Triple is a method for multi-hop question answering that enhances multi-hop reasoning for RAG models. It begins with question-associated retrieved documents, from which a knowledge graph generator creates a knowledge graph containing supporting evidence. An autoregressive reasoning chain constructor, using demonstrations by default, builds adaptive-length reasoning chains from that graph. These chains guide triple ranking and selection and identify a subset of relevant retrieved documents for answering. TRACE-Triple has a knowledge graph generator, reasoning chain constructor, triple ranker, and triple selector; it uses three reasoning chains by default. Across the HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue development sets, it outperforms IRCoT in reported EM and F1 results and achieves up to a 14.03% average maximum EM improvement over using all retrieved documents. Its performance initially improves as the number of reasoning chains increases, then stabilizes; removing demonstrations or using fixed demonstrations decreases performance. Adaptive-length chains significantly outperform fixed-length chains, while results also depend on the graph generator, constructor, ranker, selector, maximum chain length, and number of candidate triples.

l: TRACE-Doc, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: TRACE-Doc is a TRACE variant for multi-hop QA that uses adaptive-length reasoning chains to identify useful documents. It retrieves documents through triples in those chains and uses majority voting to order them. The identified documents contain significantly less noise than those for a vanilla RAG model, and TRACE-Doc achieves superior performance, including an average 13.46% Exact Match improvement over using all retrieved documents. On development sets, it reaches 69.20 EM/78.46 F1 on HotPotQA, 68.00/75.96 on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and 41.00/47.09 on MuSiQue. With a Mistral-7B-v0.1 reader, its reported results are lower across the three datasets. Ablations show that the KG generator, reasoning-chain constructor, triple ranker, and triple selector are important for retrieving relevant documents. As the number of reasoning chains increases, performance first improves and then stabilizes; adaptive chains substantially outperform fixed-length chains.

l: Triple Ranker, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

At each reasoning-chain step, it receives the current context and knowledge graph, selects top-K relevant candidate triples, and is evaluated against no ranking, DRAGON+, and E5; removing ranking lowers performance, while E5 outperforms DRAGON+.

l: triple selector, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The triple selector is a large language model with in-context learning that builds coherent reasoning chains by selecting knowledge-graph triples one at a time. It receives a question, existing knowledge triples, and a candidate set, using a prompt and a multiple-choice task to mitigate hallucination. It outputs logits for a triple distribution, or, as a black-box model without accessible logits, only an option token such as “A” or “B” to select each triple.

l: adaptive chain termination strategy, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The adaptive chain termination strategy ends a reasoning chain when no additional triples are needed. It dynamically determines optimal chain lengths and required triples, avoiding unnecessary and redundant triples to improve QA performance. Though omitted from Algorithm 1 for clarity, it can be incorporated if needed. Experiments on MuSiQue show effectiveness consistent with HotPotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA.

l: HotPotQA, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: HotPotQA is a dataset for diverse, explainable multi-hop question answering, typically requiring two to four reasoning hops and associating each question with 10 Wikipedia documents. It is one of three datasets used to evaluate TRACE and baselines; its original development set has 7,405 questions. Analyses examine reasoning-chain length, candidate triples, generated knowledge graphs, and document selection: its test-set graphs average 83.21 entities, 79.06 triples, and 1.20% density, while chain-selected documents have a 21.06% error rate versus 79.66% for original documents. Performance initially improves as more reasoning chains are used. TRACE-Triple and TRACE-Doc achieve the highest reported test performance; TRACE-Doc reports 69.20 EM and 78.46 F1 on development, with further Mistral-reader results reported for both variants.

l: 2WikiMultiHopQA, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: 2WikiMultiHopQA is a multi-hop question answering dataset whose questions are typically designed for 2–4 reasoning hops and are each associated with 10 Wikipedia documents. It is one of three datasets used with TRACE, and its original development set has 12,576 questions. Evaluations report TRACE-Triple as best on its test set, TRACE-Doc development results of 68.00 EM and 75.96 F1, reader-comparison results, and analyses in which more reasoning chains first improve results then stabilize; fixed demonstrations slightly reduce TRACE-Triple performance.

l: MuSiQue, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: MuSiQue is a multi-hop question answering dataset created through single-hop question composition. Its questions typically require two to four reasoning hops and are each associated with 20 Wikipedia documents. It is one of three multi-hop QA datasets used to evaluate TRACE; its original development set has 2,417 questions. Across reported evaluations, TRACE-Triple and TRACE-Doc outperform baselines on the test set, while ablations show reduced TRACE-Triple performance when demonstrations are removed or fixed. TRACE-Doc records 41.00 EM and 47.09 F1 on development data, with chain length affecting performance.

l: E5-Mistral, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: E5-Mistral is a triple ranker with the e5-mistral-7b-instruct Hugging Face checkpoint. It retrieves the top three most similar labelled documents to demonstrate knowledge-graph generation, and the top three most similar labelled questions with corresponding reasoning chains to demonstrate construction of a reasoning chain for a question.

l: IRCoT, TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: IRCoT is a chain-of-thought reasoning/model method used as a baseline for document retrieval and answer generation. It generates CoT sentences with LLaMA3-8B-Instruct, or thoughts/selects triples with LLaMA3-7B, and alternates thought generation with document retrieval. Its iterative autoregressive process requires multiple LLM forward propagations; reported HotPotQA development runtimes are 2.06e-3 seconds for indexing and 4.27 seconds for inference. In evaluations, it serves as a strong, best-performing baseline in the main comparison, but TRACE-Triple and TRACE-Doc outperform it in average EM and reported comparisons, partly because generated CoT sentences may be hallucinated or inaccurate. With a Mistral reader, it reports results on HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue.

l: An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This ACL 2024 long paper, “An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation,” by Kun Zhu, Xiaocheng Feng, Xiyuan Du, Yuxuan Gu, Weijiang Yu, Haotian Wang, Qianglong Chen, Zheng Chu, Jingchang Chen, and Bing Qin, addresses noisy retrieved evidence in retrieval-augmented generation. It argues that large language models can suffer hallucination, knowledge gaps, weak retrieval, and irrelevant or harmful internet material; retrieved passages may therefore degrade question-answering performance. The work frames noise filtering through Information Bottleneck theory: a filter should retain information useful for the ground output while discarding unnecessary information from retrieved passages. Its conditional mutual-information objective balances correctness and conciseness, potentially preserving the useful overlap between evidence and output or reducing irrelevant passages to empty. The paper derives an Information Bottleneck formula to evaluate filters, choose supervised fine-tuning examples, and construct reinforcement-learning rewards. Its method proceeds in two stages. Candidate passage compressions are selected for supervised fine-tuning, then Direct Preference Optimization uses Information Bottleneck-based preferences. The approach is evaluated with LLaMA2, including LLaMA2-13B, on Natural Questions, TRIVIAQA, and HOTPOTQA, using Dense Passage Retriever passages. Across these question-answering settings, the proposed SFT and DPO filtering variants improve exact-match and F1 results, reduce false errors and True-Flip-Rate, and substantially shorten evidence. RANKGPT and LONGLLMLINGUA recover some performance but generally do not exceed the non-retrieval generator, whereas the proposed filter does. Ablations indicate that jointly considering correctness and conciseness, and selecting data with the Information Bottleneck criterion, yields better filtered data and outcomes. The reported compression rate is 2.5%. The conclusion presents the system as an approximation to oracle filtering that outperforms baselines while achieving strong compression. Limitations are that effectiveness depends on a capable, especially white-box, generator and that a predictive flag and additional training iterations involve trade-offs and added cost. The ethics statement notes that filtering can mitigate toxic retrieved material but cannot guarantee its removal. Kun Zhu and Xiaocheng Feng contributed equally, and Bing Qin is the corresponding author.

l: Information Bottleneck, An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Information Bottleneck is a theory, concept, and principle for accomplishing a task with minimal information. It characterizes learning as a balance between data compression and information retention: it extracts features essential to a task, preserves information relevant to target signals or ground outputs, and discards redundant or unnecessary information. It has applications in representation learning, deep learning, document clustering, speech recognition, and summarization. In the work, it is introduced into retrieval-augmented generation as a principle and objective for filtering noise from retrieved passages, maximizing useful information while minimizing noise; it can also enable empty compression when retrieval is unnecessary or ineffective. The work provides an Information Bottleneck formula and uses its objective and IB score to balance conciseness or compression against correctness. From this basis, it supports comprehensive evaluation of noise filtering, selection of supervised fine-tuning training data, and construction of preferences or rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments report improved retrieval filtering, fewer retrieval-induced errors, and filtered training data that outperforms tested exact-search and greedy-search candidates. The conclusion presents it as a way to balance conciseness and correctness across filtering, evaluation, training-data selection, and reinforcement learning.

l: Noise Filtering, An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Noise Filtering is a filtering module for retrieval-augmented generation that compresses retrieved passages into a subset before generation, removing irrelevant, redundant, or misleading evidence. Its central aim is to preserve the precise intersection of retrieved passages and outputs while compressing irrelevant evidence to empty, balancing conciseness and correctness through an Information Bottleneck objective rather than log-likelihood-based filtering. The approach develops through SFT and DPO variants, trained with LLAMA2-7B using LORA, and experiments report fewer evidence words, reduced retrieval-induced mistakes, and comparable useful information. Remaining limitations include unsupported answering, inability to ensure generation-supporting results, and limited adaptation to compression extent.

l: retrieval-augmented generation, An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-augmented generation is a generation approach that combines large language models with relevant information retrieved from an extensive corpus during inference. It commonly concatenates retrieved passages with a query to improve output relevance, coherence, and factual accuracy. Its main practical difficulty is noisy real-world retrieval: weak retrievers and redundant or irrelevant passages can make correct answers incorrect. As retrieved evidence grows, it can also exceed context-window limits, raise computation, and reduce performance. The described work treats retrieval-augmented generation as the setting for information-bottleneck-based compression and noise filtering, aiming to retain information useful for grounded answers. Experiments supply generators with top-one or top-five DPR-retrieved passages and motivate filters that improve FFR while limiting TFR. The conclusion and limitations position the method as enhancing noise-filtering performance in retrieval-augmented generation.

s: LLAMA2 is a large language model backbone used for filtering and generation in experiments. Its 13B version serves unchanged as generator, while its 7B version is LoRA-fine-tuned for noise filtering and used as a summarization baseline. s: Natural Questions is an open-domain question answering dataset and benchmark. Evaluated on its development set with Wikipedia passages, a proposed filtering approach improves EM and F1 over direct retrieval and reduces retrieval-induced errors, lowering reported TFR from 51.0 to 17.6.

s: TRIVIAQA is an open-domain question answering dataset and benchmark used in experiments. It is evaluated on a development set with DPR-retrieved Wikipedia passages, where direct retrieval may lower LLAMA2-13B EM, while the proposed approach improves EM and F1 over non-retrieval generation.

l: HOTPOTQA, An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: HOTPOTQA is an open-domain, multi-hop question answering dataset and benchmark. It evaluates approaches using retrieved Wikipedia passages; in reported experiments, the proposed method achieves 26.1 EM, 58.3 F1, and lower TFR than listed retrieval baselines.

s: is_a prompt compression method [extractive] LONGLLMLINGUA is evaluated as a prompt-compression filtering baseline. It partially restores EM, F1, and IB performance after retrieval, but it generally remains below the non-retrieval generator and the proposed information-bottleneck approach.

s: is_a question answering task Open-domain question answering is evaluated on Natural Questions and TRIVIAQA. The experiments show that LLAMA2-13B has limited performance without retrieval and can be harmed by noisy retrieved content, while filtering improves both answer accuracy and robustness.

s: Direct Preference Optimization, a recent iteration of reinforcement learning from human feedback, trains a noise filter from IB-score-ranked compression candidates, beginning with a reference policy and favoring lower scores.

s: LLaMA2-13B is used as the generator in the reported open-domain question-answering experiments. With the proposed SFT and DPO filters, it achieves higher EM and F1 scores than retrieval without filtering while using much shorter compressed evidence.

s: A compression-evaluation metric ranging from 9α to 1; it combines reconstruction and ground-output probabilities, with lower scores indicating better filtration and guiding SFT selection and DPO preferences.

s: Dense Passage Retriever is a retriever that retrieves top five non-overlapping 100-word Wikipedia passages for three datasets; recall varies substantially, with strongest development recall for TRIVIAQA.

s: Compression rate is a measure in an extractive filtering toy experiment: it reaches 2.5% on Natural Questions and 2.6% on TRIVIAQA, reducing irrelevant content and cost; retained length strongly relates to conciseness.
